| | Matt Olson's 2025 results fell short of his peak power standards, but remained consistent in other areas. For the fourth year in a row, the 32-year-old played in all 162 games and flirted with another 30/100/100 season. His 2026 projections still forecast elite home run totals and strong RBI production, supported by consistent barrel rates and everyday cleanup duties in Atlanta. Olson's 2025 batting average (.272) was buoyed by a .333 BABIP, so expect regression to around the .250 mark this year. His power floor is among the safest at the position. Olson profiles as a reliable early-round source of HR and RBI, particularly valuable in formats that de-emphasize average. Kelly Kirby - FantasyPros | |

item.dc:creator: Vlad Sedler
item.description: The 2025 season provided ideal outcomes for fantasy managers who invested in elite starting pitchers. item.content:encoded:
The 2025 season provided ideal outcomes for fantasy managers who invested in elite starting pitchers. That season, Tarik Skubal, Paul Skenes, Garrett Crochet and Zack Wheeler were the top four pitchers drafted. Per our Fantasy Player Rater, Skubal ($35.5), Crochet ($32.8) and Skenes ($30.8) finished 1-2-3 among starting pitchers in all roto formats. Wheeler finished 14th ($22.6) despite his season being cut short. As is the case every single year, to varying degrees, there were mid-round arms who produced elite roto seasons (Bryan Woo, Hunter Brown, Max Fried), as well starters such as Nathan Eovaldi, Matthew Boyd, and Trevor Rogers who provided hefty profit a as late-round picks and free agent acquisitions.
As is also the case every season, there were early-round landmines. Cole Ragans, Blake Snell, and Corbin Burnes all missed at least two-thirds of the season due to injuries. Logan Gilbert investors certainly weren’t thrilled about his abbreviated season with only six wins. Nevertheless, dream seasons from the Crème de la crème instilled an illusion of tranquility at the top of the SP pool for 2026 drafts despite the position’s inherent risks and volatile history.
The calm ominously turned to storm on Opening Day. Paul Skenes couldn’t get out of the first inning against the Mets, allowing five earned runs, as droves of social media melodramatics scolded us: “…and that’s why you never draft pitchers early!” Skenes (174 IP – 200 K – 10 W – 3.82 – 1.12) inevitably lost “fantasy god” status as his price dropped a couple of rounds for 2027 drafts. Skubal was a top 10 pitcher with elite ratios, but did not have his usual season of dominance due to missing 5-6 starts. Crochet was an injury landmine and one of many early-round busts.
There were some wins in the second tier (Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Chris Sale) as well as disappointments (Bryan Woo, Hunter Brown, Ragans again), but what may be most memorable about last season’s starting pitcher pool was that leagues were won without having to invest in early starting pitchers at all. Of course, that only happened to managers who side-stepped the early-round hitter landmines like Aaron Judge, Ronald Acuña Jr., Vladimir Guerrero Jr., Francisco Lindor and Cal Raleigh. The two top producers – Jacob Misiorowski and Cam Schlittler – were post-100 ADP picks. Of the 19 starters who earned $14 or more in 12-team leagues, 13 had an ADP of 100+, including six with an ADP of 250 or greater.

These are the pitchers with ADPs in the first five rounds of OCs. Ohtani could technically be excluded since he was mostly used as a hitter in NFBC formats last season. He did earn nearly $14, producing sparkling ratios (1.79 ERA, 0.95 WHIP) with 95 strikeouts in 85.2 innings (14 starts). Ohtani should pitch again next season, but will be a top-three consensus fantasy pick regardless. No matter where he signs, Skubal will be the first or second SP off draft boards, along with Misiorowski. Sale, Yamamoto and Cristopher Sánchez will likely live in the Round 2 range. Sale was the SP3 in 2024, SP20 in 2025 and SP4 in 2026. Yamamoto was the SP7 and SP3 in his first two full Major League seasons. Sánchez has posted consecutive seasons of 200+ innings and a sub-3.00 ERA. Hunter Brown will be a polarizing pick in the Rounds 4-7 range coming off a 20-start season where he produced a strong 3.19 ERA, but saw his WHIP and walk rate balloon from the previous season — from 1.03 and 7.8% to 1.27 and 12.2%.
A fantasy bust in 2026, Freddy Peralta is quickly surging back up confidence meters and draft boards with his dominant playoff performances. Bryan Woo and Logan Gilbert will be slightly discounted coming off disappointing seasons, but T-Mobile Park in Seattle remains advantageous to starting pitchers (30-of-30 in MLB Park Factor for hits in 2026) and bounce-backs wouldn’t be shocking, assuming good health. Ragans underwent UCL repair surgery in July and has a 10-12 month return timetable, so he’s off our radars for the forseeable future. Jacob deGrom was slightly more human in his age-38 season, posting a career-worst 4.20 ERA, albeit with a 3.11 FIP, 3.14 xFIP and 3.15 SIERA.
Fried’s UCL is “in a good place” according to NY Daily News writer, Gary Phillips. Logan Webb is no longer the position’s Iron Man and could fall out of the top 100 ADP, though he will always have supporters. A healthy Webb could provide profit at a reasonable cost.

The 61-120 ADP range was quite the mixed bag.
Dylan Cease and Jesús Luzardo were studs and will be drafted in the top 50 in most formats.
Wheeler recovered thoroughly from his thoracic outlet procedure and produced yet another $20+ season: 162 IP (28 starts) – 193 K – 14 W – 3.00 – 1.05. He has been the best pitcher in the Majors since 2021, leading in wins (79), ERA (2.92) and second in strikeouts (1,234) behind Cease’s 1,345.
Chase Burns will be highly coveted after his masterful performance over his first full season (154.1 IP – 185 K – 15 W – 2.86 – 1.17) and will be drafted among the top 12 to 15 starters. Nolan McLean will be slightly cheaper than Burns after his first full and successful season in the Majors. Cases made against either this offseason will start with concerns about their lack of elite control and potential WHIP damage at Tier 2 SP prices. Eury Pérez is in this boat as well after posting a 10.3% walk rate and a 1.21 WHIP, though don’t expect to pay anything but a premium for the coveted fireballer who will turn 24 in April.
Joe Ryan should be a solid pick among the top 100 as well. Though he may never have that 180+ IP dream season where good health and all the cards align, Ryan has been a dependable fantasy stud, posting a K-BB% over 20% for four straight seasons and has made between 23 and 30 starts over his first five full seasons.
There were quite a few negative value guys in this range, which was quite shocking for some: George Kirby, Kyle Bradish, Framber Valdez, Kevin Gausman and Emmet Sheehan. Kirby is quickly becoming persona non grata in the fantasy community, posting a painful 1.40 WHIP last season and two straight years with a 4.00+ ERA. Bradish’s WHIP (1.42) was even worse than Kirby’s as he did most of his damage after the All-Star break, posting a 5.29 ERA and a .398 wOBA in those final 10 starts before getting shelved due to lower abdominal pain and being diagnosed with a sports hernia. Gausman compiled 30+ starts for a sixth consecutive season. Despite nearly all of his rate stats and underlying metrics matching last season’s, Gausman posted a 4.51 ERA, with an xFIP and SIERA over a full run lower. I’ll remind myself of how solid everything looked under the hood for Gausman and would consider targeting him again in 2027 drafts. Sheehan isn’t going to fly under the radar this draft season despite last year’s poor results. The key here, of course, is Sheehan having a rotation spot. He dominated in his time down in Triple-A and fired three gems for the Dodgers in September (0.53 ERA, 24:3 K:BB in 17 innings/3 starts).

Rasmussen and Gray sported matching 2.72 ERAs and finished as top 12 starters. Both will be highly coveted by drafters and I’m sure that the Rasmussen helium will take soar him into the third round of 12-teamers, especially with the glow of playoff glory. Gray dazzled with a below-average strikeout rate of 21.8%, which was 6-7% lower than his two previous seasons in St. Louis. Because of some peripheral drop-offs and his age (36), don’t be surprised to see Gray fall into some offseason bust articles.
Imanaga had three massive disaster starts in the second half of May, but his overall production was strong and his control is on the border of elite. He posted a 5.2% walk rate and a 24.6% strikeout rate and owns a 19.4% K-BB% over three Major League seasons. He’s a free agent who the Cubs would love to re-sign, though we should expect the Padres to show strong interest. I’m definitely interested in Imanaga next season.
Robbie Ray is also a free agent who should generate offseason interest. He will certainly experience a price dip from the 100s to the 200s after a visit from the control boogie man (12% BB) last season.
Gavin Williams led the AL in strikeouts, fueled by an impressive 15% swinging-strike rate. More importantly, he reduced a near-12% walk rate down to below nine percent last season. Williams won’t be cheap in drafts, and rightfully so.

There were some stretches of fantasy usefulness from several in this tier, but no big payoffs. Ryan Weathers’ first season in the AL was a roller coaster ride, but mostly positive. He finished the season with a 3.60 ERA aligned with peripherals (3.50 SIERA, 3.44 xFIP), a 1.22 WHIP, and a 18.5% K-BB%. His roto value was weighed down by just five victories. Carlos Rodón was a properly discounted stash who was activated on May 10 and pitched nine starts before elbow inflammation reappeared and he missed two months of the summer. The end-of-season line was good (2.67 ERA, 1.06 WHIP, 26.8% K in 16 starts). His 11.2% walk rate wasn’t and it was his first season over 10% in the post-Covid era. An air of trepidation will likely always remain for Rodón because of his elbow, which may result in a 2027 discount, with profitability a likely outcome if his UCL stays intact.
Jack Flaherty and Zac Gallen are falling semi-stars who were unmitigated disasters last season. Gallen finished with a 3-9 record and a 6.07 ERA in 105.1 innings. Flaherty threw just 88.1 innings and had a 4.48 ERA with his typical high strikeout rate (26%). Flaherty and Gallen are both free agents. They’ll be more appealing to real-life teams than to fantasy managers.
Tanner Bibee makes 30 starts a season, but is essentially just a thrower now. He has posted an ERA over 4.00 for a second straight season and has seen his strikeout rate reduced in three consecutive seasons — from 26.3% to 21.3% to 19%. Bibee has three years left on his 5yr, $45M deal.
Trey Yesavage was certainly trending toward Miz and Schlittler range this winter and early spring, earning a minimum pick of 113 in Online Championships. Yesavage ADP helium was quickly popped a week before Opening Day because of right shoulder impingement. In the Too Early Meatball draft in August, Yesavage was drafted in the 15th round, and this is a 15-team format. It would hard to imagine Yesavage not rising up boards back into the top 150 overall. He has a spot in the Jays rotation so all he needs know is to stay healthy.

A long list of names, so we’ll just touch on a few of them. Among the studs who provided tremendous profit were Cade Cavalli, Reid Detmers, Nick Martinez, Payton Tolle, and the impenetrable Eduardo Rodriguez, who pulled off 17 wins with a 2.89 ERA despite a much higher xFIP (4.44) and SIERA (4.62) and the lowest BABIP (.274 of his career). I don’t usually mess with the peripheral gods and will stubbornly skip over him in early drafts. Cade Cavalli had an epic run after the All-Star break, posting a 90:16 K:BB and a 1.90 ERA over his final 12 starts. Reid Detmers was having a decent season, but really began to shine when the Angels fired pitching coach Mike Maddux. Over those final 8 starts, Detmers posted a 4-0 record with a 1.62 ERA and an impressive 55:5 K:BB. Angels fans are hoping that the new regime under new owner Stan Kroenke will bring the organization from the basement to at least the living room. Interim GM John Mozeliak will stay in the role for now and help the Angels find a permanent GM and a new manager, since Kurt Suzuki is one-and-done.
A $1.20 earning shouldn’t detract from the admiration that Clay Holmes should receive after Round 15 in 12-teamers. He produced a respectable 3.29 ERA, but his low value was impacted by a low strikeout rate (18.6%), six wins, and time spent on the IL, which led to just 18 starts on the season. Michael Wacha was stellar yet again, earning $10 in 12-team NFBC roto leagues as the SP29. Taj Bradley, Troy Melton, Ian Seymour, Justin Wrobleski, and Michael Soroka all had some strong stretches of production that helped fantasy managers, especially those who got out of the Wrobleski business before that ship began to sank. Seymour and Melton are already earning some early 2027 draft love, getting scooped up among the top 50 starters in the 150-175 ADP range — a price that is likely to surge as we move through the heart of draft season.
Finally, a shout out to FAAB stud Sean Burke who broke out in a big way. He produced a 3.34 ERA, a 1.20 WHIP and punched out 185 batters over 172.1 innings. Burke had a scorching-hot nine-start run from June 18 through August 11 where he rocked a 1.60 ERA and struck out 79, with just 11 walks over 62 innings. He had some rough starts, but was still worth every free agent penny. Based on some of the prices (2-5% of budget), it almost felt like pennies were what were being spent.
It’s always a good idea to dig into player stats not long after the season has ended. It helps avoid building biases that may fester, resonate, and solidify within our draft tendencies for the coming draft season. When we wait too long into the winter to review individual player profiles, we increase the likelihood of outside influences manipulating our valuations of players — whether it’s articles that do a good job of convincing a player is a boon or a bust, social media bandwaggoning, or ADP data itself. We don’t have to decide between Ashcraft and McLean now, but if we’re equipped with the details of their stats, underlying metrics, velocity trends, pitch mix changes, Stuff, and healthy history, we can limit emotion and bias from our decision-making and make optimal, objective decisions during the heart of draft season.
Vlad writes for RotoGraphs and is the head of fantasy baseball content at FTN Fantasy. He is a Tout Wars Expert League champ, member of the CDM Fantasy Sports Hall of Fame and has been nominated for FSWA writing awards six times. Vlad has been playing fantasy baseball since 1995, winning 42 NFBC leagues since 2012 and ranking in the top percentile in NFBC’s Online Championship contest (33% win rate, 52% cash rate; 64 leagues). Much to the chagrin of his colleagues and most baseball aficionados, Vlad is a lifelong Dodgers fan who claims his first gut call at age 9 was Kirk Gibson’s 1988 World Series home run. item.content:encoded:
For the first time in his eight-year major league career, Arizona Diamondbacks right-hander Zac Gallen found himself trotting out of the bullpen and taking the mound in the seventh inning. He had never once pitched in relief in MLB — even following an opener.
Gallen, after a brutal start to his 2026 season and a multi-month layoff due to elbow inflammation, was moved to a bullpen role following an unsuccessful return debut.
That decision was officially announced on September 13, and it took five days for him to make his first relief outing.
Unfortunately for Gallen and the Diamondbacks, it came in a game that already looked bleak. The hard-hitting New York Yankees had already pummeled starter Eduardo Rodriguez for six runs in 5.1 innings. Arizona trailed 7-2 when Gallen took the mound.
How Zac Gallen performed in first bullpen appearance
Gallen pitched the final three innings of Friday night's game, allowing two runs in the process. Only one was earned, due to a throwing error by first baseman Pavin Smith on a ground ball that should have been an out. He threw 68 pitches, 41 of them landing for strikes.
The issue? Gallen allowed two base hits and walked two batters in the proces. His velocity was up a touch on his slider, which was his most primarily-used offering. He was able to pick up four whiffs on 12 swings with that pitch.
His four-seam fastball, however, was once again close to nonexistent. Of those 68 pitches, only 10 were four-seams. He did not manage to pick up a whiff on six swings, and was only able to land two of them in the zone for called strikes.
It's not exactly an encouraging or discouraging sign to see Gallen perform this way in a relief capacity. He did not showcase elite-level improvement with his velocity or movement, and he struggled with base traffic, as well as putting away batters. His ERA went down, but only to 6.12 on the year.
Unfortunately, even if Gallen had pitched three elite innings, the Diamondbacks would not have had much of a chance to engineer a victory. Trailing by five runs before they even came up to bat, Arizona never closed the deficit to lower than four runs on the night. They lost 9-2.
With the San Diego Padres taking down the Miami Marlins, 8-2, Arizona now sits five games back of the third and final Wild Card berth, with just eight games left on the schedule. Time is quickly running out.
An Arizona native, Alex D'Agostino is the Publisher and credentialed reporter for Arizona Diamondbacks On SI. He previously served as Deputy Editor for Arizona Diamondbacks and Arizona Cardinals On SI and covered both teams for FanSided. Alex also writes for PHNX Sports. Follow Alex on X/Twitter @AlexDagAZ.
